title: "Design choices"
description: >
  Why the defaults are what they are, which decisions a function makes for
  you and where it records them, and which settings can and cannot change a
  result.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r libs}
library(anovakit)
```

Every anovakit function follows the same rules about what it prints, which
settings can change a result, and what it decides for you. Each is shown below
on a small example; for the object itself see [Working with
results](results.html).

## Nothing prints

No analysis function writes to the console, and no plot is drawn as a side
effect. Warnings and messages raised while fitting by car, emmeans,
sandwich, afex and base R's model functions are captured and recorded in
`$notes` instead of reaching the console. Here a logistic regression with
separation in one group prints nothing, and the second of its notes
describes the problem:

```{r silent}
sep <- data.frame(
  group = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 10),
  y     = c(rep(0, 10), rep(c(0, 1), 5), rep(c(0, 1, 1, 1, 1), 2))
)
out <- capture.output(fit_sep <- anova_bin(sep, "y", "group", plots = FALSE))
length(out)
writeLines(strwrap(fit_sep$notes[2], 72))
```

`verbose = TRUE` reports progress through `message()`, so
`suppressMessages()` silences it. Plots are built and stored in `$plots`; they
appear only when you print one.

## `conf_level` sets every interval

One argument sets the level of every interval in the tables a function
returns: group and marginal means, pairwise differences, effect sizes, odds and
rate ratios, simple slopes and the error bars in the plots.

```{r conf-level}
fit90 <- anova_glm(chickwts, "weight", "feed", conf_level = 0.90,
                   plots = FALSE)
fit90$conf_level
head(fit90$posthoc[, c("contrast", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high")], 3)
```

It does not reach `$emmeans_object`. That is emmeans' own reference grid,
and it carries emmeans' default level of 0.95. Pass the level to the function
that summarises the grid, such as `confint()`; given to `contrast()` it has no
effect on the intervals:

```{r conf-level-grid}
ctl <- emmeans::contrast(fit90$emmeans_object, "trt.vs.ctrl")
confint(ctl, level = fit90$conf_level)
```

## Type II by default, and what Type III means

`anova_manova()`, `anova_bin()`, `anova_count()` and `anova_glm()` report
Type II tests by default. Each main effect is tested after the other main
effects, and the result does not depend on how the factors are coded.
`anova_ancova()` and `anova_rm()` default to Type III; the
[ANCOVA](ancova.html) and [repeated measures](repeated-measures.html)
walkthroughs explain their tables. The type used is printed in the heading and
stored in `attr(fit$anova, "ss_type")`.

When you ask for `type = "III"`, the model is fitted under sum-to-zero
contrasts. In a model with an interaction, a Type III main-effect row tests
the main effect only under those contrasts. Under R's default treatment
contrasts, `car::Anova(type = 3)` tests the simple effect of each factor at the
reference level of the other, and still labels the table Type III.

The `warpbreaks` data with the first five rows removed make an unbalanced
two-way design:

```{r type-3}
wb <- warpbreaks[-(1:5), ]
t3 <- anova_glm(wb, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"), interaction = TRUE,
                type = "III", plots = FALSE)
unlist(t3$model$contrasts)
t3$anova
```

The same model fitted with treatment contrasts and passed to car gives a
different `wool` row, which is the effect of wool at `tension = "L"` only:

```{r type-3-car}
car::Anova(lm(breaks ~ wool * tension, data = wb), type = 3)["wool", ]
```

A model with aliased coefficients, such as one with an empty cell, has no
Type III tests. The function then computes Type II tests, and the heading,
`$method` and `$notes` say so.

## Covariates are centred

`anova_ancova()` mean-centres every covariate before fitting
(`center_covariates = TRUE`), and `anova_manova()` centres its covariates too.
Centring always moves the intercept to the covariate mean. When the model
contains a group-by-covariate term and `type = "III"`, it also moves the group
row, because that row then tests the groups at covariate = 0. On a baseline
score distributed around 100, zero is far from the data:

```{r centring}
set.seed(2024)
n <- 240
trial <- data.frame(
  arm      = factor(rep(c("placebo", "low", "high"), each = n / 3)),
  baseline = rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 12)
)
effect <- c(placebo = 0, low = 3, high = 7)[as.character(trial$arm)]
trial$score <- 0.6 * trial$baseline + effect + rnorm(n, 0, 6)

centred <- anova_ancova(trial, "score", "arm", "baseline",
                        force_interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)
uncentred <- anova_ancova(trial, "score", "arm", "baseline",
                          force_interaction = TRUE,
                          center_covariates = FALSE, plots = FALSE)
data.frame(term        = centred$anova$term,
           p_centred   = signif(centred$anova$p_value, 3),
           p_uncentred = signif(uncentred$anova$p_value, 3))
all.equal(centred$emmeans, uncentred$emmeans)
```

On the same rows, the `arm` row has p =
`r format(signif(centred$anova$p_value[2], 2))` centred and p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", uncentred$anova$p_value[2])` uncentred. The other rows and the
marginal means are the same, because `$emmeans`, `$posthoc` and
`$simple_slopes` are always evaluated with every covariate at its mean (a 0/1
covariate included). In the additive model, and under Type II, centring does
not change the group row. The means subtracted are in `$covariate_means`.

## The ANCOVA model is chosen by a test unless you fix it

By default `anova_ancova()` chooses between the additive and the
separate-slopes model with a homogeneity-of-slopes test on the same data, and
records the choice in `$notes`. The p-values that follow do not allow for that
selection. If the test misses a real slope difference, the group row and
`$posthoc` reject more often than their nominal level: somewhat so when the
groups were randomised, and far more so when the groups' covariate means
differ, which `$notes` points out. `force_interaction = TRUE` fixes the
separate-slopes model in advance and avoids the selection step. With several
grouping factors, `anova_ancova()` fits their interaction by default
(`interaction = TRUE`), as a factorial ANCOVA does. The [ANCOVA
walkthrough](ancova.html) covers both choices in detail.

## Comparisons follow the model

When grouping factors enter a model additively (`interaction = FALSE`, the
default except in `anova_ancova()`), `$emmeans` and `$posthoc` are reported for
each factor on its own, averaged over the others, with a `term` column and one
multiplicity family per factor. Comparing every cell would repeat each
main-effect difference once per level of the other factors, and adjust for
comparisons that carry no extra information.

```{r additive}
additive <- anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                      plots = FALSE)
additive$emmeans[, c("term", "wool", "tension", "estimate")]
additive$posthoc[, c("term", "contrast", "p_adjusted")]
```

When the model contains the interaction, the cells are compared:

```{r interaction}
cells <- anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                   interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)
nrow(cells$emmeans)
nrow(cells$posthoc)
```

A level combination with no data is left out when the model cannot estimate
it, and named in `$notes` when the model estimates it by extrapolation (as an
additive model does). With no model to follow, `anova_welch()` and
`anova_kw()` combine the grouping columns into one factor of the cells that
contain data and compare those.

## Every argument is named

No modelling function has a `...` argument except `anova_rm()`, and that one
accepts only `fun_aggregate`, `observed`, `type` and
`anova_table = list(p_adjust_method = )`, passed to `afex::aov_ez()`. Anything
else is refused by name rather than ignored:

```{r dots}
rm_data <- data.frame(id = rep(1:6, each = 2), time = rep(c("pre", "post"), 6),
                      y = c(5, 7, 4, 6, 6, 9, 5, 5, 7, 8, 4, 7))
try(anova_rm(rm_data, "y", "id", "time", es = "pes"))
```

Every argument that reaches a fitting call is named, so nothing can be passed
through that overrides a decision the function has made. A `contrasts =`
argument, for example, would defeat `type = "III"` while the table still said
Type III, so it is an unused argument:

```{r contrasts}
try(anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", contrasts = list()))
```

A column may play only one role (response, group, covariate, weights, offset
or subject):

```{r roles}
try(anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", weights = "breaks"))
```

Prior weights are given as a column name rather than a vector, so they are
subsetted with the data and stay aligned when a row is dropped. Rows with a
weight of zero contribute nothing to the fit. They are dropped and counted in
`$n_removed`, so that row counts, robust standard errors and information
criteria agree with the fit:

```{r zero-weights}
w <- warpbreaks
w$wt <- 1
w$wt[1:3] <- 0
anova_glm(w, "breaks", "tension", weights = "wt", plots = FALSE)$n_removed
```

## Global settings do not change results

Options set for some other analysis in the same session do not change a fit's
results. `afex::afex_options()` cannot change an `anova_rm()` fit, because
the type, the contrasts and the emmeans model are all set explicitly. The
`emmeans::emm_options()` settings that change a result (adjustment, sidedness,
null, degrees of freedom, scale) are cleared for the duration of the fit; only
computational limits such as `rg.limit` are kept, so you can still let a large
grid through.

The
global `contrasts` option can change how a Type II model's coefficients are
coded, but not its tests, marginal means or comparisons; `type = "III"` always
fits under sum-to-zero contrasts, and odds and rate ratios always come from a
treatment-coded fit. Here an `emm_options()` setting that turns off every
adjustment leaves the Tukey adjustment in place:

```{r emm-options}
emmeans::emm_options(contrast = list(adjust = "none"))
tension <- anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", plots = FALSE)
tension$posthoc[, c("contrast", "p_value", "p_adjusted", "adjustment")]
emmeans::emm_options(contrast = NULL)
```

The only option of its own that anovakit reads is `anovakit.theme`, which
sets the base theme of every plot and changes no result; the [plots
guide](visuals.html) shows how to use it.

## Assumption checks match the method

Each function checks the assumptions its own method makes. `anova_welch()`
tests normality within each group rather than on pooled residuals. Pooling
groups with different variances produces a mixture that can fail a normality
test when every group is normal, which would argue against the method being
used. For the same reason `anova_rm()` tests the within-subject residuals in
each within-subject cell.

```{r welch-normality}
welch <- anova_welch(chickwts, "weight", "feed", plots = FALSE)
welch$assumptions$normality[, c("group", "n", "statistic", "p_value")]
```

`anova_kw()` assumes no distribution, so it runs no checks unless you ask
with `diagnostics = TRUE`:

```{r kw-checks}
length(anova_kw(chickwts, "weight", "feed", plots = FALSE)$assumptions)
names(anova_kw(chickwts, "weight", "feed", plots = FALSE,
               diagnostics = TRUE)$assumptions)
```

The [diagnostics guide](diagnostics.html) lists every check by function and
what to do when one fails.

## Robust standard errors

`vcov_type = "HC0"` to `"HC4"` on `anova_ancova()`, `anova_bin()`,
`anova_count()` and `anova_glm()` changes the standard errors in the
coefficient table and in the marginal means and comparisons. In
`anova_ancova()` it also reaches the F tests (as robust Wald F tests) and the
simple slopes, and in the other three the omnibus table when
`test_statistic = "Wald"`. Likelihood-ratio tests rest on the model. Where
fitted values sit on the boundary (separation, an all-zero group) or a cell has
one observation, the model-based covariance is used, with a note. [Weights and
robust standard errors](weights.html) gives the rules, including how
whole-number weights are treated as frequency weights.

## Multiplicity adjustments depend on the method

`anova_welch()` and `anova_kw()` compare groups directly and accept the
`p.adjust()` methods, defaulting to `"holm"` and `"BH"`. The other six take
their comparisons from emmeans, which also offers `"tukey"` (their
default), `"sidak"`, `"scheffe"` and `"dunnettx"`. Every `$posthoc` table
reports the unadjusted p-value in `p_value`, the adjusted one in `p_adjusted`
and the method in `adjustment`, as the table above shows.

The intervals in `$posthoc` from the emmeans-based functions are
simultaneous. emmeans cannot turn a step-down method such as Holm's into
intervals and uses Bonferroni intervals instead; `$notes` says when that
happens. `anova_welch()` reports a per-comparison interval for each pair.

## Notes record every decision

Whenever a function chooses something on your behalf, it says so in `$notes`:
the model chosen by a slopes test or a dispersion statistic, a centred
covariate, dropped rows or subjects, a fallback from Type III to Type II, an
odds ratio that is not identified. The ANCOVA above, fitted without
`force_interaction`, records two decisions:

```{r decisions}
writeLines(anova_ancova(trial, "score", "arm", "baseline", plots = FALSE)$notes)
```

Missing optional packages are recorded the same way. Without MASS,
`anova_count(model = "auto")` fits a quasi-Poisson model where it would have
chosen a negative binomial, and without sandwich a `vcov_type` request falls
back to model-based standard errors; each records the fallback in `$notes`.
`anova_rm()` without afex, and `anova_count(model = "negbin")` without
MASS, stop with an error instead.

[Working with results](results.html#the-notes) shows how to read and search
the notes, and how `$data_used` and `$n_removed` account for every row you
supplied.
